facts.value: Among the proponents of the more relativist viewpoint was E. H. Carr, whose 'What Is History?' examined how historical and social contexts impact the way historians choose and analyse facts.
Some scholars argue that recognising the subjective nature of historical sources has the benefit of opening up new areas of research and new ways of engaging with historical subjects.
Scholars advocating for this view include Richard J. Evans.
For example, some Japanese high school history textbooks have faced various criticisms for downplaying Japan's colonial and wartime activities.
They are sometimes grouped under the label auxiliary sciences of history.
